common_name: Moonlight Witch Hazel (Pale Yellow Fragrant Winter-Blooming Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; witch hazel flower buds need real winter chill to open well, so bloom is most reliable where winters stay reliably cold through midwinter.

directions: Moonlight bears some of the palest flowers of any witch hazel cultivar, its slender, crinkled petals opening a soft primrose to sulfur-yellow with a faint reddish-purple flush at the petal base, glowing gently against bare branches on mild days in mid to late winter. The loosely branched, somewhat coarse-textured habit gives it a more open, airy silhouette than tighter cultivars like Arnold Promise, and its sweet, light fragrance carries well on still winter air. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, siting it where low winter light can backlight the translucent petals, and prune lightly right after flowering only if shaping is needed.

common_name: Aphrodite Witch Hazel (Vigorous Orange-Red Fragrant Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Aphrodite is a vigorous, wide-spreading Belgian selection that flowers most heavily with at least a half day of direct sun.

directions: Aphrodite is an exceptionally free-flowering, RHS Award of Garden Merit witch hazel cultivar, smothering its bare winter branches in dense clusters of crimped, ribbon-shaped, orange-red petals set off by a reddish-purple calyx, with each spidery bloom curling shut on the coldest days and unfurling again as temperatures rise above roughly 40°F. Its vigorous, wide-spreading lateral branching gives it a fuller, denser silhouette than many intermedia cultivars, and dark green summer foliage turns attractive yellow and red tones before dropping to reveal the next winter's flower show. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune lightly right after flowering only if shaping is needed, since witch hazel resents both drought and waterlogged soil.

common_name: Blue Shadow Fothergilla (Intense Blue-Green Foliage Witch Alder)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Blue Shadow is propagated by softwood cuttings and holds its striking blue-green foliage color best with at least a half day of direct sun.

directions: Blue Shadow is the most widely grown selection of intermediate fothergilla, prized above all for summer foliage of an unusually intense, powdery blue-green that ranks among the most striking blue tones of any deciduous shrub, deepening the effect of its fragrant, creamy-white bottlebrush flower spikes that open on bare stems in early spring before the leaves emerge. In autumn the blue-green leaves ignite into a fiery mix of red, orange, and yellow, giving the shrub genuine three-season interest in a compact, rounded form more restrained than the straight species. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, and pair with azaleas, mountain laurels, and other acid-loving shrubs in a woodland border or foundation planting.

common_name: J.L. Pennock White Enkianthus (Gold Medal Fall-Color Selection)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; J.L. Pennock is a slow-growing selection prized for fall color that begins about two weeks earlier and holds longer than the species.

directions: J.L. Pennock, a Pennsylvania Horticultural Society Gold Medal winner, is a refined selection of white enkianthus valued for dainty clusters of pure white, urn-shaped flowers that nod discreetly beneath finely serrated foliage in mid-spring. Its standout feature is fall color that develops roughly two weeks ahead of the species and lingers through the end of the season, passing from a hint of burgundy in early autumn to a brilliant red or glowing yellow-orange across the whole shrub. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, siting it in the middle layer of an azalea or rhododendron border where its slow, dense growth and long fall display can be fully appreciated.

common_name: Veitch's Winter Hazel (Butter-Yellow Weeping-Raceme Winter Hazel)

planting.note: Plant in acidic, humus-rich soil in a sheltered, partly shaded site so the very early spring flower racemes escape late frost damage; young reddish shoots are glabrous and slightly tender when new growth emerges.

directions: Veitch's winter hazel forms a rounded, bushy shrub with reddish young stems and weeping racemes, roughly 3 inches long, of delicately scented, butter-yellow flowers that open on bare branches from late winter into early spring, ahead of the obovate to elliptic foliage. Grow in acidic to neutral, well-drained soil enriched with leaf mold or compost, in a site sheltered from harsh wind and late frost, which can damage the precocious blooms. Partial shade with some morning sun brings out the best flowering and keeps summer foliage clean, while deep, occasional watering during dry spells protects the shallow root system from stress; prune only to remove damaged wood right after flowering, since next year's buds form on the current season's growth.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
